paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify a coherent group when only a few examples of that group are available. The learner receives positive examples and a much larger pool of instances, then seeks a rule that separates similar instances from the rest. The challenge is to describe the intended group without requiring labeled examples of everything outside it.

The authors formulate this task as a rate-distortion tradeoff. This gives the problem a mathematical structure in which competing demands on the representation can be analyzed precisely. Their formulation also leads to an efficient algorithm, connecting the theoretical account to a practical method for selecting instances.

The algorithm compares favorably with two earlier one-class methods. The authors also extend the model to clustering situations where background clutter can weaken the coherence of the resulting groups. In that setting, removing clutter is part of obtaining purer clusters. The contribution therefore links learning from a few positive examples with clustering that explicitly accommodates unwanted background instances.
icml-2008-a-rate-distortion-one-class-mo.tldr: A rate-distortion formulation yields an efficient one-class classifier and extends to clustering that removes background clutter.

paragraphs: The paper brings several language-processing tasks into a single convolutional neural network. Given a sentence, the architecture produces grammatical tags, phrase chunks, named entity tags, semantic roles, information about similar words, and a language-model judgment of whether the sentence makes grammatical and semantic sense. These outputs cover multiple aspects of sentence understanding within one learned system.

The network learns the tasks jointly through shared weights. This means that training for one task can influence parameters also used by other tasks. Most tasks learn from labeled examples, while the language model learns from unlabeled text. Sharing parameters provides a route for that unlabeled text to help the tasks that otherwise depend on annotations.

The authors report that both joint task learning and learning from unlabeled text improve generalization on the shared tasks, producing state-of-the-art performance. The significance is that the architecture combines two sources of useful training information: supervision from related tasks and language patterns available without labels. The reported gains support their use together in a unified language-processing model.
icml-2008-a-unified-architecture-for-nat.tldr: A shared convolutional network learns multiple language tasks jointly and uses unlabeled text to improve their generalization.

paragraphs: An agent can compute an optimal policy when it knows the transition probabilities and rewards of its decision problem. In practice, experts may struggle to specify those probabilities accurately. Learning them through interaction is another option, but exploration can be lengthy and costly. This paper asks how an imperfect initial model can help direct that exploration.

The proposed method examines how sensitive the optimal policy is to changes in transitions and rewards. It then concentrates exploration on regions where those changes matter most to the policy. The initial specification is allowed to be inaccurate, so it serves as a starting point for deciding where further experience is especially relevant.

The authors report that this strategy performs well on several control and planning problems. Its central idea is to connect exploration to the decisions the agent ultimately needs to make. Model errors matter differently depending on whether they affect the preferred behavior, and policy sensitivity provides a way to focus learning around that distinction.
icml-2008-active-reinforcement-learning-.tldr: The method directs exploration toward transitions and rewards whose changes most affect the optimal policy.

paragraphs: The paper studies a hidden-state model for sequences in which the number of underlying states is unknown. The hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model can learn the size of its state space from data. The authors identify limitations in its original formulation when modeling dynamics that should persist smoothly over time.

They introduce a sticky extension that supports state persistence and more robust learning of such dynamics. The formulation also uses Dirichlet process mixtures to represent more complex emission distributions, including distributions with several modes. This allows observations associated with a state to have richer patterns without giving up the model's flexible treatment of hidden states.

The authors additionally develop a sampling procedure that jointly redraws the entire state sequence using a truncated approximation of the Dirichlet process. They report greatly improved mixing rates, meaning the sampler moves more effectively through possible explanations of the data. Experiments on synthetic sequences and a speaker diarization database demonstrate advantages of the sticky extension and support its usefulness for real-world sequence modeling.
icml-2008-an-hdp-hmm-for-systems-with-st.tldr: A sticky HDP-HMM improves modeling of persistent states and combines richer observations with more effective sequence sampling.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when an environment has a large number of possible states. The representation of those states matters because it determines what structure a learner can reuse across experiences. This paper introduces Object-Oriented Markov Decision Processes, which describe environments through objects and their interactions.

The representation creates opportunities to generalize by expressing the environment in terms of its constituent entities and their relationships. The authors pair it with a learning algorithm for deterministic object-oriented environments. They prove a polynomial bound on the algorithm's sample complexity, giving a theoretical account of how much experience learning requires within that setting.

The paper illustrates performance gains in the Taxi domain and a real-life video game. These demonstrations connect the representational proposal to concrete learning tasks. The contribution includes both a way to describe structured environments and an algorithm with a learning-efficiency guarantee. The deterministic setting is an explicit part of the algorithm and bound, so that guarantee should be understood within that scope.
icml-2008-an-object-oriented-representat.tldr: Object-Oriented MDPs represent objects and interactions, enabling a deterministic learning algorithm with polynomial sample complexity.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a vision system can estimate the precision of the maps it constructs. Its example is the creation of digital elevation models through stereo matching, where corresponding image information is used to triangulate real-world points. The authors demonstrate that errors in these map-making tasks have a sparse structure.

They combine that sparsity with a geometric theory of errors they had developed. Together, these ingredients allow autonomous agents to calculate their own precision without relying on ground truth. This addresses the problem of assessing a reconstruction when an independently known correct version is unavailable for direct comparison.

The authors connect the approach to sparse signal reconstruction and compressed sensing. The key connection is the usefulness of sparse error structure for recovering information about uncertainty in the reconstruction. Their theoretical contribution extends the autonomy previously established for three-dimensional reconstruction to the errors of those reconstructions. The claimed self-assessment depends on the sparse structure and geometric theory developed in this setting.
icml-2008-autonomous-geometric-precision.tldr: Sparse errors and geometric error theory let vision agents estimate reconstruction precision independently of ground truth.

paragraphs: The infinite hidden Markov model extends sequence modeling to a setting with a flexible hidden-state space. Working with that model requires an inference procedure that can handle its potentially unbounded collection of states. This paper introduces beam sampling as a way to carry out that inference efficiently.

The method combines slice sampling with dynamic programming. Slice sampling restricts the states considered at each time step to a finite set. Dynamic programming then makes it possible to sample complete hidden-state trajectories efficiently. The two components address complementary parts of the problem: controlling the states under consideration and coordinating inference across the sequence.

The authors report that beam sampling typically outperforms the Gibbs sampler and offers greater robustness. They demonstrate its use in changepoint detection and text prediction. These applications show how the inference method supports both identifying changes in a sequence and predicting its content. The performance claim is typical rather than universal, while the methodological contribution is the combination of finite per-step computation with whole-trajectory sampling.
icml-2008-beam-sampling-for-the-infinite.tldr: Beam sampling combines slice sampling and dynamic programming for efficient, typically more robust inference in infinite hidden Markov models.

paragraphs: The paper introduces linear classifiers that track confidence in their parameters as learning proceeds. Learning therefore involves both estimating useful weights and increasing confidence in those estimates. This adds an explicit account of parameter uncertainty to the classifier's representation of what it has learned from examples.

The authors investigate an online algorithm that maintains a Gaussian distribution over weight vectors. Each new training instance updates the distribution's mean and variance. The mean represents the current weight estimates, while the variance carries confidence information. Updating both quantities lets the model revise its predictions and its certainty about the parameters within the same learning process.

Evaluations on several natural language processing tasks show improvements over the online and batch methods used for comparison. The authors also report faster learning in the online setting and better classifier combination following parallel training. These findings give confidence information two practical roles: supporting learning as examples arrive and helping combine classifiers that were trained separately. The reported advantages are empirical results from the evaluated tasks.
icml-2008-confidence-weighted-linear-cla.tldr: An online linear classifier updates a Gaussian distribution over weights to learn predictions and parameter confidence together.

paragraphs: The paper develops faster algorithms for projecting vectors onto an L1-ball, a constraint that limits the sum of absolute coordinate values. Projection is a recurring operation in constrained learning: after an update, the vector must be brought back into the permitted region. Its cost can matter greatly in high-dimensional problems.

The first algorithm computes an exact projection in O(n) time for a vector with n coordinates. The second takes O(k log(n)) time in the setting where k coordinates are perturbed outside the ball. That second setting is especially relevant when online updates involve sparse features, as in text categorization.

Experiments cover both batch and online learning. The authors report that stochastic gradient projection variants using these procedures outperform optimization methods including interior point methods. They also find that online gradient updates with L1 projections outperform the EG algorithm while producing highly sparse models. The contribution makes a mathematical constraint cheaper to enforce and demonstrates that the improved operation can translate into practical learning benefits.
icml-2008-efficient-projections-onto-the.tldr: Efficient L1-ball projection algorithms improve constrained learning speed and support highly sparse online models.

paragraphs: Point-process observations consist of events that provide sparse, noisy evidence about an underlying intensity function. The paper focuses on recovering that function over time. A continuous estimate can be easier to analyze than the events themselves because it describes the intensity driving the process across the temporal domain.

Gaussian processes provide the inference framework, but a naive implementation has demanding memory and runtime requirements. The authors identify this computational burden as a barrier to using the approach on reasonably sized problems. Their work therefore targets the calculation needed to obtain the intensity estimate, making the inference procedure more practical.

For a class of renewal processes, the authors develop methods that exploit the particular problem structure. They report eliminating the memory burden and reducing solution time by orders of magnitude. The stated scope matters: these are specialized methods for the identified class of processes. Their significance is that problem-specific computation can make Gaussian-process intensity estimation accessible where a straightforward implementation would be computationally infeasible.
icml-2008-fast-gaussian-process-methods-.tldr: Specialized Gaussian-process methods dramatically reduce the computational burden of intensity estimation for a class of renewal processes.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning a decision function when some training attributes are missing. One motivating situation is combining data from several sources that record different subsets of attributes. The resulting training collection contains useful information, but no single source necessarily supplies every value the classifier could use.

The authors formulate a joint optimization problem that learns the classifier while also treating the distribution of missing values as a free parameter. This makes the treatment of unobserved attributes part of the learning problem itself. The distribution and final decision function are determined together, linking possible completions of the data to the classifier being trained.

A central theoretical result shows that the optimal distribution places its mass on finitely many atoms, or discrete support points. This finite structure leads to an algorithm despite the distributional formulation's broad range of possible missing values. The paper reports empirical results on benchmark datasets and an email spam application. Together, the optimization and finite-support result provide a concrete route from incomplete training records to a learned classifier.
icml-2008-learning-from-incomplete-data-.tldr: Jointly optimizing a classifier and missing-value distribution yields an optimum with finite support and a corresponding learning algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classifiers whose inputs become less reliable after training. A deployed system may encounter missing or corrupted features even when that kind of noise was absent from its training data. The learning objective is therefore to obtain a classifier that remains robust to this form of classification-time disruption.

The authors develop two approaches. The first uses linear programming to solve an approximation of the learning problem. They analyze how tight that approximation is and prove statistical risk bounds. This provides both a computational route to a solution and a theoretical account of its relationship to the learning objective.

The second approach formulates an online version of the problem and adapts the Perceptron to address it. An online-to-batch conversion then turns that procedure into a statistical learning algorithm. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The contribution combines optimization-based and online-learning routes to handling the same practical mismatch: feature information available during training may become unavailable or unreliable when predictions are needed.
icml-2008-learning-to-classify-with-miss.tldr: Linear-programming and modified-Perceptron methods learn classifiers robust to missing or corrupted features at prediction time.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines several kernels and learns their weights during training. The paper identifies a restriction of the standard approach: each kernel receives the same weight throughout the input space. A kernel that is useful for one region therefore cannot receive a different emphasis solely because an example lies elsewhere.

The proposed localized method introduces a gating model that selects appropriate kernels locally. The gate and kernel-based classifier are optimized jointly, so decisions about local kernel use develop alongside the prediction model. The method can also use several copies of the same kernel function, with each copy localized to a different region.

Experiments on ten benchmark datasets and two bioinformatics datasets support the approach's applicability. Compared with ordinary multiple kernel learning, it achieves statistically similar accuracy while storing fewer support vectors. On the bioinformatics datasets, multiple localized linear kernels improve accuracy over a single linear kernel. The findings connect local adaptation both to a more compact classifier representation and, in the stated comparison, to improved predictions.
icml-2008-localized-multiple-kernel-lear.tldr: Jointly learned local kernel selection achieves comparable MKL accuracy with fewer support vectors and improves some linear-kernel results.

paragraphs: The paper develops a rule-learning algorithm for classification through probability estimation. Decision rules are attractive because they are simple and interpretable. The authors build on that advantage by using individual rules as the component classifiers of an ensemble, giving multiple rules a role in the final predictive model.

The ensemble is constructed greedily by minimizing negative log-likelihood. This objective connects the selection of rules to estimating class probabilities: the learning procedure seeks rule combinations that better account for the observed class labels probabilistically. The approach therefore gives rule induction an explicit probability-estimation objective, rather than treating the final output only as a class assignment.

The paper compares the method with SLIPPER, LRI, and RuleFit. Its stated contribution is the construction of a rule ensemble through likelihood optimization, alongside those empirical comparisons. The abstract does not claim a particular comparative winner. The approach matters because it brings interpretable rule components into a common statistical objective, tying how the ensemble is built to the probability estimates it is intended to produce.
icml-2008-maximum-likelihood-rule-ensemb.tldr: The method builds interpretable rule ensembles by greedily optimizing likelihood to estimate class probabilities.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a topic model can learn from large amounts of data arriving over long periods while obeying a fixed memory budget. It develops a memory-bounded version of variational expectation-maximization, an algorithm for approximate inference. The memory constraint is maintained as part of the learning process.

The algorithm alternates between model building and model compression. During building, Bayesian model selection lets the internal representation grow by adding topics as more data arrives. During compression, data items are merged into groups, and the algorithm retains their sufficient statistics. This reduces the information that must remain explicitly stored.

The two phases allow the model to expand its representation while periodically reducing its storage demands. Empirically, the resulting procedure handles datasets orders of magnitude larger than the standard batch version. The finding demonstrates the practical value of combining adaptive model growth with compression under a specified memory limit. The contribution concerns approximate inference designed around sustained learning when retaining an ever-growing representation would exceed available memory.
icml-2008-memory-bounded-inference-in-to.tldr: Alternating topic-model growth and statistical compression enables approximate inference under a fixed memory budget.

paragraphs: The paper introduces OCAS, an optimized cutting-plane algorithm for training linear support vector machines. Its computational effort scales linearly with the number of training examples. The aim is to make large training problems faster to solve while obtaining the same precise support vector solution as competing solvers.

The empirical evaluation reports substantial improvements over SVMLight, SVMPerf, and BMRM. On some datasets, speedups exceed 1,000 relative to SVMLight and reach 20 relative to SVMPerf. OCAS also often converges faster during early optimization than SGD and Pegasos. These are reported comparative results, with the strongest speedups applying to particular datasets.

Parallel OCAS trains on 15 million examples occupying about 32 GB in 671 seconds. The abstract also reports that a competing string-kernel SVM takes 97,484 seconds on a 10-million-example subset. That comparison involves different model configurations and dataset sizes. Together, the results demonstrate the algorithm's practical scale and show that faster optimization can coexist with obtaining a precise linear SVM solution.
icml-2008-optimized-cutting-plane-algori.tldr: OCAS accelerates precise linear SVM training, with substantial reported speedups and a parallel demonstration on 15 million examples.

paragraphs: Learning to rank requires a model to order instances or express preferences among them. Obtaining labels can be expensive because someone must provide relative orderings over alternatives. The paper addresses this burden by choosing which unlabeled data should receive attention during training, rather than treating all potential labels as equally valuable.

The authors propose an active-learning framework for both SVM-based and boosting-based ranking methods. Their sampling criterion maximizes an estimated loss differential over unlabeled data. In practical terms, the method uses an estimate of how much a labeling choice could improve the learning objective to guide the next request for information.

Experiments on two benchmark corpora show substantially reduced labeling effort and rapid improvements in performance. The reported advantage reaches as much as 30% relative improvement over margin-based sampling. That figure describes the strongest stated improvement, not a uniform gain across settings. The contribution is a ranking-specific way to direct labeling effort toward estimated learning benefit, supported by results for the evaluated corpora.
icml-2008-optimizing-estimated-loss-redu.tldr: Selecting ranking labels by estimated loss reduction lowers labeling effort and improves performance in two benchmark evaluations.

paragraphs: Cost curves visualize binary classifier performance under different operating conditions. A curve alone does not convey how reliable its estimated costs are. This paper addresses that uncertainty by constructing confidence intervals for both a classifier's cost and the difference in cost between two classifiers.

Bootstrap resampling of a test set provides one route to such intervals. The authors derive the exact bootstrap distributions of the relevant quantities at individual operating conditions and use them to calculate confidence intervals. The resulting intervals for cost differences support assessing whether one classifier performs significantly better than another under the condition being considered.

The evaluation measures coverage accuracy: how well the confidence intervals achieve their intended coverage in simulations. The authors report excellent simulation results. The contribution is a precise account of the bootstrap distribution underlying pointwise cost comparisons. Exactness here refers to that bootstrap distribution; the empirical coverage evaluation separately assesses the behavior of the resulting intervals. This connects performance visualization with a more explicit treatment of statistical reliability.
icml-2008-pointwise-exact-bootstrap-dist.tldr: Exact pointwise bootstrap distributions provide confidence intervals for classifier costs and cost differences, with strong simulated coverage.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a classifier that represents the target class with a polyhedron, a shape bounded by multiple flat faces. Its training procedure uses limited information about subclasses among the negative examples. Each hyperplane classifier is designed to distinguish positive examples from one of those negative subclasses.

The hyperplanes are optimized jointly so that they collectively describe the target class. The authors attribute robustness to the flat faces and flexibility to having multiple faces. This combines simple individual boundaries into a shape able to accommodate more complex data. The available negative subclass information gives the separate boundaries distinct classification roles.

The proposed classifier is evaluated on a real-world colon dataset in a computer-aided detection case study. The authors report improved prediction accuracy and runtime speedups when the model operates within a real-time cascade. They also compare it with benchmark classifiers. The contribution connects a structured geometric representation to both prediction and execution efficiency, with the stated evidence coming from this target-detection application.
icml-2008-polyhedral-classifier-for-targ.tldr: Jointly learned polyhedral boundaries use negative subclasses to improve target detection and accelerate cascaded execution.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when rare but significant events occur independently of the agent's actions. Sampling these events at their natural frequency can make learning slow and variable. Important consequences may receive little representation in the experience available to estimate the value of a policy.

The approach assumes access to a simulator in which rare-event probabilities can be changed artificially. The authors use importance sampling to learn from the altered simulation data while accounting for the changed probabilities. They develop policy-evaluation algorithms for both tabular value representations and representations that use function approximation.

The authors prove convergence for both versions. For the tabular setting, they also analyze bias and variance relative to temporal-difference learning. Empirical evaluation uses random Markov Decision Processes and a large network-planning task. The contribution provides a principled way to make rare events more available during simulation-based policy evaluation. Its simulator access and action-independent event assumptions are integral to the setting in which the methods are developed.
icml-2008-reinforcement-learning-in-the-.tldr: Importance-sampling policy evaluation uses adjustable rare-event simulation probabilities, with convergence proved for tabular and function-approximation methods.

paragraphs: Partially observable decision models support planning when an agent cannot directly observe the full state of its environment. They can balance actions that gather knowledge with actions that earn reward. However, specifying the many parameters of such a model from domain expertise alone can be difficult.

The paper treats uncertainty about those parameters as part of the hidden state. This produces a larger model-uncertainty POMDP in which planning must account for both the environment and incomplete knowledge of its governing model. The authors develop an approximate planning algorithm for this expanded problem, making model uncertainty an explicit element of decision-making.

They combine that approximation with model-directed queries so that the planner can actively learn useful policies. Demonstrations on several standard POMDP problems support the approach. The contribution connects parameter learning with planning under partial observability: information gathering is guided by a model that represents uncertainty about its own parameters. The method is approximate, so the optimal tradeoff associated with POMDP planning should not be read as an exact guarantee for this algorithm.
icml-2008-reinforcement-learning-with-li.tldr: An approximate planner treats uncertain POMDP parameters as hidden state and uses model-directed queries to learn policies actively.

paragraphs: The paper introduces self-taught clustering: grouping a small unlabeled target dataset with help from a much larger unlabeled auxiliary dataset. The two datasets may differ in their topic distributions. The motivation is that the target collection alone may be too small to support learning a useful feature representation.

The proposed algorithm uses co-clustering to process the target and auxiliary data simultaneously. A common set of features lets representations learned from the auxiliary collection influence the target collection. The method therefore transfers information through shared features even when the auxiliary examples do not match the target's topical distribution.

Under the resulting representation, target clustering can improve. Image-clustering experiments show that the algorithm can greatly outperform several state-of-the-art clustering methods when using irrelevant unlabeled auxiliary data. The finding supports the possibility that data need not directly match the target topic to help organize it. The reported benefit depends on learning useful shared features, and the experimental result establishes that this transfer can work in the evaluated image-clustering setting.
icml-2008-self-taught-clustering-a027fa9.tldr: Co-clustering transfers useful features from auxiliary unlabeled data to improve clustering of a small target collection.

paragraphs: The paper uses algorithmic stability to study transductive regression. Stability concerns how sensitive a learning procedure is to changes in its training information. The authors use this perspective to derive generalization bounds for several families of algorithms, providing theoretical tools for assessing how their predictions may behave beyond the observed labels.

Their analysis draws on both convexity and closed-form solutions. It enables comparisons among the algorithms and suggests that some existing methods might lack stability. The authors also prescribe a technique for making them stable. The result is therefore both diagnostic and constructive: it helps identify potential sensitivity and offers a way to address it.

Experiments with local transductive regression demonstrate that the bounds can help with model selection. In particular, they support choosing the radius of the neighborhood used by the algorithm. This gives the theoretical analysis a concrete operational role. The paper connects stability guarantees to an actual modeling choice, showing how a bound can guide the scale of information used for local predictions.
icml-2008-stability-of-transductive-regr.tldr: Stability analysis yields transductive regression bounds, a stabilization technique, and practical guidance for choosing local neighborhood size.

paragraphs: Computing leave-one-out error requires evaluating predictions when individual training examples are excluded. For support vector machines, the paper develops a stopping condition tailored to this evaluation objective. The condition identifies when an intermediate solver result already gives the output needed for the leave-one-out calculation.

The proposed sufficient condition guarantees that this output matches the output of the optimal SVM trained without the excluded point. A simple addition to a general SVM training algorithm enables an equivalent stopping criterion. This allows optimization to stop once the relevant prediction is certified, while preserving exactness of the leave-one-out error computation.

A comprehensive empirical evaluation reports consistent speedups, reaching a factor of 13 for the linear kernel. The contribution is to align computational stopping with the purpose of the calculation: obtaining the correct held-out output. The condition is sufficient, so its guarantee applies when it is satisfied without claiming that it identifies every possible opportunity to stop. The reported speedups show that this guarantee can save substantial computation in practice.
icml-2008-stopping-conditions-for-exact-.tldr: A sufficient stopping condition speeds exact SVM leave-one-out evaluation by certifying the needed prediction before optimization finishes.

paragraphs: Structured prediction applications can require inference that is too complex to perform exactly during training. This paper studies how to train structural support vector machines under that constraint. It examines two families of approximation: undergenerating methods, including greedy procedures, and overgenerating methods, including relaxations.

Undergenerating methods search a restricted collection of possibilities, while overgenerating methods expand the optimization space through a relaxation. The authors develop and analyze algorithms from both families, using theoretical arguments and empirical evaluation. Their investigation focuses on fully connected pairwise Markov random fields, providing a concrete setting for comparing the consequences of these training choices.

The authors find theoretical advantages for overgenerating methods and greater empirical robustness relative to undergenerating approaches. They also report that models trained with relaxations favor non-fractional predictions when used with relaxed predictors. This suggests that training can influence whether a relaxed prediction procedure produces a discrete result. The contribution shows that the form of approximation matters for both learning behavior and the outputs obtained at prediction time.
icml-2008-training-structural-svms-when-.tldr: Comparing approximate structural SVM training methods reveals theoretical and empirical advantages for overgenerating relaxations.
